cells.tense: You are bearing the weight right now without breaking and without bracing.
cells.act: feel it alongside them and keep your own side
cells.ask: Next time someone you love is in it, sit with them a while. Take in what they're carrying. Stay yourself while you do. No fixing, no merging — two people, one hard thing.
cells.core:
You can take weight. Put something heavy on you and you hold it, without hardening and without leaning in so far you disappear. Years of repeated work have left you with more room in you than most people have. People feel it. They bring you the hard stuff because you don't flinch and you don't take over.

But holding isn't the same as going still. The other half is staying in contact while you bear it. Next time someone leans on you, let yourself be reached by what they're carrying and stay on your own side of it — near, not fused. That isn't softer. It's what lets the two of you keep breathing in the same room.
cells.sheetLine: You hold the weight and still let it reach you.
cells.verb: Enduring what presses down and keeping your shape
cells.place: In a practice you keep at alone, through repetition

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead you are already bracing for weight that has not arrived.
cells.act: put it in proportion, not in punishment
cells.ask: This week, name what you're braced for and ask what's actually owed there. Give that much. Then stop, before the extra. No paying for a future that hasn't happened.
cells.core:
The strength is real. The trouble is you're spending it early. In your practice you tighten before there's anything to tighten against — the rope pulled taut with nothing on the other end. It feels like readiness. From outside it looks like rigidity, and the body pays either way. What you're carrying is getting carried past the point where carrying helps.

So bring something back to size. Name what you're braced for, ask what the moment actually calls for, do exactly that, and set the rest down. Not less effort. The right amount, no more. Where every obligation has turned into a debt to be worked off, give what's fair and quit the arithmetic. Strength that can loosen holds longer.
cells.sheetLine: You're gripping past what the moment asks of you.
cells.verb: Enduring what presses down and keeping your shape
cells.place: In a practice you keep at alone, through repetition

cells.tense: For a while now, when the weight comes down, something in you has slipped out from under it.
cells.act: release it on purpose, not by losing it
cells.ask: Take a load you're still holding that finished its work already. Set it down on purpose. Not losing it — letting it go. Rest your hands a while and see what the room feels like.
cells.core:
Right now, holding feels dangerous, so you don't. When pressure comes, something folds instead of bearing, and the practice that used to steady you has gone thin. That isn't a flaw in you. It's a load that kept being carried with nowhere to set it down, and the bearing part went quiet. The strength has not left. It's stalled, waiting on something to be put down before it can stand again.

That's the way back: let go on purpose. Find a responsibility, a half-finished effort, an outcome you keep checking — something done, or something that was yours only by habit — and set it down. Not because you failed. Because it's finished. Rest your hands and notice you're still on your feet. The bearing comes back once there's room for it.
cells.sheetLine: You folded because there was nowhere to set it down.
cells.verb: Enduring what presses down and keeping your shape
cells.place: In a practice you keep at alone, through repetition

cells.tense: This strength keeps running, and you have not once counted yourself as its owner.
cells.act: remember what drew you and face it again
cells.ask: Think back to what first pulled you into this practice — the reason, before it became routine. Go face that again this week. Know plainly what you want there. Privately. Nobody else has to hear it.
cells.core:
You carry more than you credit yourself with. The steady work, the showing up, the strength that keeps things standing — you'd call it just what you do. Anyone standing next to you calls it that, if not the whole structure. Same when something drops you: you don't see how much you were under, or that going down was honest.

So go back to the reason. There's a person, a craft, a want — whatever it was that pulled you into this before it turned into repetition. Face it again this week and let yourself want it plainly, in private. That original pull is what all this runs on. Remembering it puts your hand back where it has been the whole time.
cells.sheetLine: The strength is yours. You just haven't signed for it.
cells.verb: Enduring what presses down and keeping your shape
cells.place: In a practice you keep at alone, through repetition

attempts.check: The draft most at risk of overreach is the Too Little cell: it may read into the person a history behind the collapse, and the record only supports that holding currently feels dangerous. A reader could say, 'I'm not collapsed; I'm just tired,' and the ask should still land — releasing one thing held past its use is useful even if my read is off. The sentence that serves the writer is any tidy image of a 'door behind you' — cut it; the person needs plain talk about what is held, not a metaphor about where they stand.
